cues.text: Failure mode and effects analysis, often called F M E A,
can organize a discussion.
This course uses a fictional three-level scale for severity,
occurrence and difficulty of detection.
These numbers are ordinal teaching categories, not measured probabilities.
They are not official regulatory limits.
The interactive exercise makes the arithmetic visible while keeping the
rationale and unresolved high-severity concerns beside the result.
In this exercise, higher severity means more serious potential harm.
Higher occurrence means the failure is more plausible given the available
evidence.
Higher detection score means it is harder to discover the failure before
its consequence.
Real projects need operational definitions tailored to the scenario.
A team should agree those definitions before scoring.
The labels lower and higher alone are not sufficient for an approved site
assessment.
Multiply three by one by two and the result is six.
Multiply one by three by two and the result is also six.
Yet the first scenario has a higher severity category.
The chart shows equal total scores with different component patterns.
Equal products do not establish equivalent risk or acceptable controls.
Review the scenario, severity, uncertainty and control options rather than
letting one number decide.
Suppose an independent alarm is proposed.
Do not lower the detection score merely because the alarm appears on a
drawing.
Determine whether it detects the relevant failure,
whether someone will respond and whether that response is timely.
Verify the control and reassess residual risk.
The activity asks you to compare two scoring rationales and explain which
assumptions need evidence.
No score in this lesson automatically authorizes release.
